panels.title: Longer technical tasks at 80% success
panels.period: Model release dates 2023-03-14 to 2026-04-07; archived TH1.1 file retrieved 2026-10-22
panels.measure: Estimated task length in human-expert minutes at 80% predicted success, on METR's technical task suite.
panels.headline: 53 seconds to 3.1 hours
panels.finding: The archived estimates rise from 0.889561 minutes for GPT-4 to 185.911829 minutes for Claude Mythos Preview (early). The latter's published 95% interval is 1.62 to 6.64 hours.
caveats: Human-expert task time, not AI runtime or hours of autonomous operation.
Mainly software, machine-learning and cybersecurity tasks with explicit success criteria; not whole jobs or a measure of all intellectual work.
Intervals are wide; tools and scaffolds vary. Model release dates are not evaluation or publication dates.
This is an archived benchmark, not a current frontier ranking. It excludes newer benchmark versions and models absent from this file.
panels.transformation: Select every source result released on or after 2023-01-01 whose benchmark_name is METR-Horizon-v1.1. Copy release_date and metrics.p80_horizon_length estimate/ci_low/ci_high without scaling. Sort by release date, descending estimate for ties. Mark successive strictly higher estimates as records; join only these records. Keep all model points and uncertainty. Convert minutes to seconds or hours only in display labels; do not fit, smooth, interpolate or forecast.
panels.locator: YAML: results.<model_id>.release_date and results.<model_id>.metrics.p80_horizon_length.{estimate,ci_low,ci_high}. METR's chart JS divides these fields by 60 for hours and labels the interval 95% CI.
panels.verificationNote: Fresh source YAML parsed with Ruby Psych and checked against src/capability.js: all 23 dates and 69 numerical fields match exactly; no eligible models are missing. The file has 26 models in total, including three pre-2023 TH1.0 entries that are excluded. Source webpage and chart JS confirm the interval label and minute-to-hour conversion. Models are taken from this file only; no TH2 figures or invented model sequence added.

chart.linePolicy: Join record-high rows only; show all 23 model points. The line is a guide between observed model estimates.

uncertainty.display: error bars or explicit point tooltips; never treat as extra series

chart.yScaleNote: Logarithmic minutes accommodate the full range and all uncertainty endpoints. A linear scale is also valid if clearly labeled and its domain includes 398.514614 minutes when intervals are drawn.
chart.rounding: Source precision retained; headline units rounded.

reviewFlags: Keep TH1.1 and 80% success in the visible label; do not replace with TH2 or 50% values.
Record highs are derived for this panel from p80 estimates, not from the YAML is_sota field.
The latest plotted model was released 2026-04-07; METR's update log says it was added 2026-05-08.

panels.title: Employment by age in the most AI-exposed occupations
panels.sourceName: Stanford Digital Economy Lab and ADP Research, Canaries Dashboard
panels.period: Monthly observations September 2021 to August 2026; source vintage 2026-09-17, released 2026-09-23
panels.measure: Employment index within each age group in occupational AI-exposure quintile 5; each group's own November 2022 employment = 100.
panels.headline: Ages 22-25: employment index 87.23
panels.finding: In August 2026, employment for ages 22-25 was 12.77% below its November 2022 level in the most exposed occupation group. Indices for ages 31 and older remained above their own baselines.
caveats: Descriptive payroll trends do not identify jobs lost because of AI.
Five-year balanced sample of ADP firms and workers matched to occupation codes; not the whole US labor market. Firm entry and exit are excluded.
Age groups are not fixed cohorts. Each line has its own baseline, so index levels do not compare headcounts.
Exposure quintiles contain equally weighted occupations, not equal numbers of workers. Do not average age-group indices without baseline employment weights.
panels.transformation: From the pinned ZIP's canaries_age_by_exposure.csv, filter exposure_quintile == 'Quintile 5 (most exposed)'. Preserve all six age columns and 60 monthly rows. Values are already indexed to 100: no further multiplication, rebasing, averaging or interpolation. Display rounded to two decimals while retaining source numbers.
panels.locator: ZIP member canaries_age_by_exposure.csv; observation_date and the six age columns; filter Quintile 5 (most exposed). Dictionary section for the underlying Employment Index, not annualized or year-over-year change files.
panels.verificationNote: Fresh pinned ZIP and manifest downloaded; all 60 dates and 360 values match src/comparison-data.js exactly, including floating-point tails. All six November 2022 indices equal 100. ZIP, CSV and dictionary hashes also match the prior recorded hashes. The live dashboard was updated 2026-10-21, but its newer release is intentionally not mixed into this September vintage.

chart.confidenceIntervalNote: The download does not supply confidence intervals for these descriptive series.

reviewFlags: Visible period must end August 2026 and identify the September release; do not call this the latest dashboard.
Do not attach the paper's separate relative high-versus-low-exposure employment estimate to these age-series lines.
The capability/work pairing does not establish that benchmark progress caused the observed employment changes.

panels.title: Self-reported AI use at work
panels.period: Eight survey-month labels, May 2023 to August 2026; primary HTML table retrieved 2026-10-22
panels.measure: Percent of US employees aged 18+ working full or part time for organizations who report AI use at work at each frequency.
panels.headline: 32% report using AI a few times a week or more
panels.finding: Gallup's table shows frequent use rising from 11% in May 2023 to 32% in August 2026. Over the same waves, any use rose from 21% to 53% and daily use from 4% to 16%.
caveats: Self-reported use, not hours automated, productivity, or the share of jobs replaced.
Daily users are included in frequent users, who are included in total users. Do not sum or stack the three groups.
Weighted probability-panel surveys of employees of organizations; not all adults or all self-employed people. Individual respondents are not followed as a fixed cohort in this chart.
The source table runs through August 2026, while page prose still says May 2026 and its embedded version-1 download stops in August 2025.
panels.transformation: Extract the single primary HTML table with headers Use of AI / Daily AI users / Frequent AI users / Total AI users. Convert M/1/YY labels to ISO dates for chart positions; they identify survey months, not one-day fieldwork. Retain the published whole-percent values and all eight accessible rows, without borrowing waves from OWID, other polls or Gallup articles.
panels.locator: Gallup indicator HTML, noscript table.c-datawrapper__data whose caption is '1 in 10 U.S. Employees Use AI Daily in Their Role'; rows 5/1/23 through 8/1/26. Source methods define frequencies and date labels.

panels.title: Unaided exam scores after AI-assisted practice
panels.period: Fall 2023-2024 school term; article published 2025-06-25; affiliation correction 2025-08-20
panels.measure: Adjusted intention-to-treat difference in subsequent unassisted mathematics exam score versus the no-AI control, rescaled from 0-1 to points on a 0-100 scale.
panels.headline: 5.4 points lower after GPT Base practice
panels.finding: The GPT Base estimate is -5.4 points, about 17% of the control group's mean score. GPT Tutor's estimate is -0.4 points and is not statistically distinguishable from control.
caveats: One Turkish high school, grades 9-11, with immediate exams after practice; this is not evidence of permanent skill loss or an estimate for US workers.
Table 1 has 2,848 student-session observations, not 2,848 distinct students; randomization and robust standard errors are at classroom level.
The tutor result does not establish equivalence or prove no effect. Its safeguards bundle teacher-provided content with prompting changes.
Both tools improved assisted practice performance; the featured outcome is the separate exam without AI.
panels.transformation: Read Table 1 column (2): GPT Base coefficient -0.054, clustered SE 0.022; GPT Tutor coefficient -0.004, SE 0.013; control mean 0.321. Multiply scores and SEs by 100. The paper's rounded 17% relative reduction agrees with 100 * (-0.054 / 0.321) = -16.82%. No confidence interval endpoints are needed for this numeric-block presentation.
panels.locator: Publisher HTML Table 1, Exam perf column (2), with classroom-clustered SE footnote; matching author PDF printed page 10, PDF page index 9. Abstract and paragraph after Table 1 state the 17% result.
panels.verificationNote: The publisher's accessible HTML and author PDF text agree on coefficients, SEs, control mean and observation count. The existing -5.4 and -0.4 point values are correct. The August 2025 correction, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2518204122, corrects Osbert Bastani's affiliation, not the results. This audit checks published table values; it does not rerun the regressions or independently validate participant-level data.

chart.units: score points on a rescaled 0-100 exam scale
chart.displaySecondary: Guided GPT Tutor: no clear difference
chart.confidenceIntervalNote: Use numeric blocks. Prior approximate normal intervals are intentionally omitted; their source SEs are retained for auditability.
chart.comparison: Each treatment versus the no-AI control; no direct GPT Base-versus-GPT Tutor significance test inferred.

verification.correctionVerification: Publisher links the correction; its full affiliation-only notice was accessible in the primary PMC search result. Opening PMC directly subsequently returned a CAPTCHA.

reviewFlags: Proposed presentation simplification: retain the original numeric score effects but omit calculated interval bars and endpoints from the compact panel.
17% is relative to the control mean, not a 17-percentage-point or 17-point score loss.
A guided-tutor nonsignificant effect is not a demonstrated zero effect.
The adoption/skills pairing spans different countries, ages, settings and dates; it supplies no population-level effect of rising workplace use.
Human review pending.

panels.title: Deezer's reported share of fully AI-generated uploads
panels.sourceName: Deezer Newsroom, six dated company reports
panels.period: Reports from 2025-01-24 to 2026-04-20; selected non-peak daily-intake reports
panels.measure: Reported percent of tracks delivered daily to Deezer that its detector identifies as fully AI-generated.
panels.headline: About 10% to about 44% of daily uploads
panels.finding: Six company reports show a rising reported share of detected fully AI-generated tracks in daily deliveries. They describe Deezer's intake, not the composition of all music or the industry.
caveats: Report dates are not fixed measurement windows; these are selected announcements, not a daily or monthly statistical series.
Some numbers are approximations and others thresholds. Preserve the qualifiers with every point; 18 and 28 are lower thresholds, not exact shares.
Detector coverage and accuracy over time are not documented as constant. These are company reports, not an independently reproduced content audit.
Daily uploads are a flow of incoming tracks, not the stock of catalog tracks or the share people listen to.
panels.transformation: Transcribe share and publication date from each English-language release, retaining qualifiers. Prefer opening body text over inconsistent stronger wording in notes; use the introductory reported 34% for November. Add the verified November report missing from the original five-point chart. Do not derive shares from rounded track counts. Exclude repeated announcements and later peak-day statistics.
panels.locator: Each chart row links its primary release; exact paragraph locations and source hashes are in sources. April 2026 opening paragraph supplies approximately 44%.
panels.verificationNote: All five original report dates, values and qualifiers are supported by the primary releases. A sixth, 2025-11-12, explicitly reports 34% and is added. The English November release reports about 50,000 tracks versus about 40,000 in its French counterpart; both report 34%, so no count series is used. July and October 2026 releases explicitly qualify more than 50% as a peak-day share and are excluded from this series.

chart.units: percent of daily track deliveries to Deezer
chart.linePolicy: Markers are reported values or threshold anchors. Optional dashed straight guides only; no interpolation, fitted growth rate or forecast. The qualifier must appear in each point label or tooltip.
chart.confidenceIntervalNote: No sampling intervals supplied; the word 'over' is not an uncertainty interval.

panels.title: AI-generated music's reported share of Deezer streams
panels.period: Reported 2026-04-20; precise observation window not disclosed
panels.measure: Company-reported share of all Deezer streams attributed to fully AI-generated tracks.
panels.headline: 1-3% of streams
panels.finding: The April release reports a 1-3% stream share alongside about 44% of daily uploads. Different denominators prevent interpreting their ratio as a listening conversion rate.
caveats: Reported range, not a confidence interval, time series, or point estimate. Do not substitute its 2% midpoint.
Recorded streams include fraudulent activity; this is not verified human listening or a royalty share.
Deezer excludes detected AI music from recommendations and editorial playlists, so this is not unrestricted consumer preference.
The release does not specify a sampling window or enough fraud-adjustment detail to reconstruct an organic-listening share.
panels.transformation: Transcribe the endpoints 1 and 3 from the April 20 opening paragraph and notes to editors. Keep the April snapshot with the April upload endpoint; do not average the range or combine it with a different vintage's fraud rate.
panels.locator: Opening paragraph beginning Paris, April 20, 2026; repeated under Notes to editors, AI and fraud.
panels.verificationNote: Both endpoints are explicitly reported in the primary source and match the original comparison data. July and October releases repeat the range, but that repetition does not identify a new observation window or support a stream-share trend. The April body says 85% fraud while its notes refer to up to 85% in 2025, so no current fraud-adjusted estimate is calculated.

chart.comparisonNote: The uploads panel has a daily-intake denominator; this panel has an all-streams denominator.

reviewFlags: Retain a numeric range block; do not create a trend or use 2% as an observed value.
Do not calculate 0.15-0.45% organic listening by multiplying this range by 15%; the fraud figure and its period do not support that calculation.
The stream snapshot is dated April 2026, not the 2026-10-22 audit date.

overallNotes: All six panels are ready for editorial integration with the specified limits. Ready means primary-source-supported for this presentation, not human-reviewed or approved for publication.
Suggested visible pairing footnote: Different populations, periods and units. Paired panels do not establish causal links.
Supported pairs: capability/work, adoption/skills, uploads/streams. These are selected indicators, not an exhaustive review or a chain from AI capability to human outcomes.

chart.data contains array rows and chart.columns defines their order. Line charts have date in column zero; series columnIndex values are zero-based. Reuse the existing chartkit. For capability, lineRows select the record line while pointRows retain all models.
Use numeric blocks for skills and streams. Skills keeps the verified -5.4/-0.4 effects but omits approximate CI endpoints; streams keeps the reported 1-3% range.

Changes needing editorial attention: add the verified November 2025 Deezer upload point; preserve Gallup's table-versus-prose/embedded-download inconsistency in source notes; visibly label METR as archived TH1.1 and Stanford as the September 2026 release.

Source hashes identify the bytes fetched on 2026-10-22, not permanent remote immutability. HTML hashes can change when a site's unrelated navigation changes; use the table hash and pinned data-file hashes for stronger checks.

No values were digitized from chart pixels. METR, Stanford and Gallup points were checked numerically against fresh source data; Bastani was checked against the published table; Deezer uses exact transcription of qualified press-release statements.
